summary:
Montserrat is a British Overseas Territory and stands under the United Kingdom's framework, including the European Convention on Human Rights and its non-discrimination and equality obligations.

Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults in private has been lawful since 2001, when the prohibitions were swept away retrospectively by an Order in Council under Sections 3(1) and 3(7) of the Caribbean Territories (Criminal Law) Order, 2000. Lesbian conduct was never an offence. Group sex and sex in public remain criminal offences for all persons.

The age of consent is 18 for homosexual activity and 16 for heterosexual activity. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read locally as same-sex therefore falls under the higher threshold of 18.

Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal. Article 10(1) of the Constitution protects only opposite-sex marriage, providing that every man and woman of marriageable age has the right to marry a person of the opposite sex and to found a family. A trans visitor's partner would not be recognised as a spouse or civil partner.

Article 16 of the Montserrat Constitution and Article 79 of the Labour Code prohibit discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation, defining 'discriminatory' as affording different treatment on grounds such as sex, sexual orientation, race, colour, language, religion or other status. Neither provision names gender identity among the enumerated grounds, which end with an open-ended 'other status'.

There are no gay bars, nightclubs or other dedicated venues on the island. Several hotels welcome gay tourists and operate non-discrimination policies, which is the main documented point of entry for a visitor seeking a welcoming environment.
tangentialFactors:
The 2001 decriminalisation was imposed from outside rather than produced locally. An Associated Press report of January 2001 records that Britain scrapped the anti-gay statutes in five Caribbean territories, Montserrat and Turks & Caicos among them, on the ground that they violated signed international human rights agreements. Local politicians and religious leaders opposed the change, which was framed as a cultural rift with London.

The island's social scene is shaped by disaster. Hurricane Hugo in 1989 and the 1995 Soufriere Hills eruption left the south uninhabitable and displaced more than half the population northward. A 2012 GlobalGayz account describes gay life as barely existing locally, with the social scene decimated.
localsOnly:
Local political and religious leaders opposed the 2001 decriminalisation and presented it as a cultural imposition from London.

For residents, Article 79 of the Labour Code governs employment and Article 16 of the Constitution governs the treatment of individuals by public authorities; the enumerated grounds are sex, sexual orientation, race, colour, language, religion or other status.

Organised community life is effectively absent. There are no dedicated venues, and a 2012 account describes gay life as barely existing on the island.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether gender identity falls within the open-ended 'other status' ground in Article 16 of the Constitution or Article 79 of the Labour Code is unresolved; no source in the inventory addresses gender-identity-specific protections or gender marker change procedures.

No trans-specific violence data for Montserrat is sourced, and no information on police or prison treatment of trans people is available.

No entry, visa or screening provisions specific to trans travellers are sourced.

The most recent source is a 2012 account of local social life; the legal provisions are drawn from an encyclopaedia entry whose currency is unresolved.
